title: Why manage risks and issues
blurb: Tell a risk from an issue and explain, with examples, what managing each one does for a project.
question: The sponsor of a new distribution warehouse tells you risk and issue management is 'paperwork that slows the team down'. What benefits would you explain to persuade them otherwise?

teach.h: Risks look forward, issues are here now
teach.body: A RISK is an uncertain event or set of circumstances that, if it occurs, would affect the achievement of one or more objectives. It can be a THREAT (negative) or an OPPORTUNITY (positive). An ISSUE has already happened (or is certain) and needs action now; in APM's tighter sense it is a problem that has breached, or is about to breach, the project manager's tolerances, so the sponsor must help resolve it. Plain English: a risk might happen; an issue is happening.

teach.h: Risk and issue: what differs, what's shared
teach.caption: A threat that occurs stops being a risk. If it breaches tolerance, it is managed as an issue.

teach.h: The core benefit: objectives become more likely
teach.body: Projects are unique and transient, so uncertainty is unavoidable. Risk management does not remove it. It makes uncertainty visible early, so the team can act before threats land and can be ready to seize opportunities. The headline benefit is that the project becomes MORE LIKELY TO ACHIEVE ITS OBJECTIVES, with fewer surprises along the way. Issue management adds control when things do go wrong: problems are dealt with promptly, at the right level.

teach.caption: All of these feed the headline benefit: a higher likelihood of achieving the objectives.

teach.body: Issues are inevitable, so the benefit lies in handling them well. Logging each issue makes it visible and owned rather than lost in emails. Prompt analysis CONTAINS THE IMPACT before it grows. Escalating issues beyond tolerance means DECISIONS ARE TAKEN AT THE RIGHT LEVEL, by someone with the authority to act. Linking resolutions to change control keeps the baseline honest. And the issue log reveals patterns: several similar issues can point to a root cause worth fixing.

teach.h: With and without risk and issue management

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: The racking supplier may miss its date, delaying go-live before the peak season

steps.label: Analyse
steps.sub: Medium probability, high impact: a priority risk

steps.label: Respond
steps.sub: Order early; agree a fallback with a second supplier

steps.label: Outcome
steps.sub: Supplier slips 3 weeks, fallback used, go-live holds

teach.caption: The business case depended on peak-season trading. Managing one risk protected it.

teach.text: Exam distractors to reject: 'risk management eliminates all risk' (it reduces and controls exposure), 'it guarantees success' (it raises the likelihood), and 'risk is only about threats' (opportunities are risks too). Also don't call something that has ALREADY happened a risk: that is an issue.

teach.body: The benefits hold in linear and iterative projects alike; what changes is the rhythm. In a linear project, early risk work feeds the business case and the size of contingency before the big commitments at decision gates. In an iterative project, short feedback loops expose risks and issues every time box, so the benefit comes from frequent small corrections rather than one large up-front analysis.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define the difference: a risk is uncertain and future; an issue has occurred and needs action.
State a benefit of risk management, e.g. objectives more likely, fewer surprises, realistic contingency.
Add a value benefit: protects the business case and exploits opportunities.
State a benefit of issue management: impact contained, decisions at the right level.
Tie each point to the scenario in the question (its deadline, budget or stakeholders).
Risk: uncertain, future, threat or opportunity. Issue: happened, needs action, beyond tolerance goes to the sponsor.
Headline benefit: a greater likelihood of achieving objectives, with fewer surprises.
Also: better decisions and plans, realistic contingency, a protected business case, captured opportunities, stakeholder confidence.
Issue management: visibility, contained impact, decisions at the right level, root causes spotted.
Risk management reduces and controls uncertainty; it never eliminates it or guarantees success.

summary: You can now distinguish a risk from an issue and explain the benefits of managing each. You can argue the case to a sceptical sponsor: objectives become more likely, contingency is realistic, the business case is protected and problems are resolved at the right level.

A.q: Which statement best describes the main benefit of risk management to a project?
options: It removes uncertainty from the project plan
It increases the likelihood of meeting objectives
It guarantees delivery within the agreed budget
It transfers accountability to the risk owners
A.why: Risk management makes uncertainty visible and managed, so the project is more likely to achieve its objectives.

whyNot.0: Uncertainty is inherent in projects; risk management controls it but cannot remove it.
whyNot.2: Nothing can guarantee delivery on budget. Risk management raises the odds, it doesn't promise an outcome.
whyNot.3: Risk owners take on responsibility for individual risks, but transferring accountability is not the purpose of the process.

A.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a risk from an issue?
options: A risk is internal; an issue comes from outside
A risk is minor; an issue is always very severe
A risk affects cost; an issue affects the schedule
A risk is uncertain; an issue has already occurred
A.why: A risk might happen in the future; an issue has happened (or is certain) and needs action now.

whyNot.0: Both risks and issues can arise inside or outside the project.
whyNot.1: Severity doesn't define the difference: there are high-impact risks and minor problems.
whyNot.2: Either can affect any objective: time, cost, quality, scope or benefits.

A.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of effective risk management?
options: Fewer unexpected events during delivery
A more realistic contingency in the budget
No further need for a change control process
Greater stakeholder confidence in the plan
A.why: Risk management doesn't replace change control. Responses to risks and issues often need change control to update the baseline.

whyNot.0: Early identification means fewer surprises: a genuine benefit.
whyNot.1: Contingency sized from analysed risks is more realistic: a genuine benefit.
whyNot.3: Visible, controlled risks build stakeholder confidence: a genuine benefit.

B.q: During a risk workshop for a software rollout, the team notes that a new cloud pricing tier might cut hosting costs if it launches before go-live. Which benefit of risk management does recording this demonstrate?
options: Removing threats before they can occur
Reducing the need for a project sponsor
Exploiting opportunities as well as threats
Shortening the risk register for monthly reviews
B.why: The cloud tier is an uncertain event with a positive effect: an opportunity. Capturing it lets the team plan to benefit if it happens.

whyNot.0: This is an upside event, not a threat, so nothing is being removed.
whyNot.1: Risk management supports the sponsor's decisions; it never replaces the sponsor.
whyNot.3: Adding opportunities makes the register more complete, not shorter.

B.q: A project manager logs each problem that breaches tolerance and passes it to the sponsor with options and a recommendation. What is the main benefit of working this way?
options: Decisions are made at the right level
The PM avoids accountability for problems
Problems no longer need any analysis
The sponsor takes over daily management
B.why: Escalating issues beyond tolerance, with options, puts the decision with someone who has the authority to act on it.

whyNot.1: The PM stays accountable for managing the project and for presenting the issue properly.
whyNot.2: Analysis is exactly what produces the options and recommendation.
whyNot.3: The sponsor decides on the escalated issue; the PM still manages day to day.

B.q: Complete the statement: risk management helps to protect the ________, because threats to the expected costs and benefits are managed before they occur.
options: communication plan
organisation chart
business case
procurement strategy
B.why: The business case justifies the project by weighing benefits against costs and risks, so managing those risks protects it.

whyNot.0: The communication plan sets out how stakeholders are informed; it isn't what cost and benefit risks threaten.
whyNot.1: An organisation chart shows roles, not the project's justification.
whyNot.3: The procurement strategy covers how goods and services are bought, not the overall justification.

C.q: The sponsor of a hospital refurbishment argues that, because the budget is fixed, the team should skip risk management and 'just get on with it'. Which is the strongest counter-argument?
options: It sizes contingency to the real risks
It lets the team avoid change requests
It moves budget control to the supplier
It replaces the need for progress reports
C.why: A fixed budget makes risk management more important: analysed risks show how much contingency is genuinely needed and where the budget is exposed.

whyNot.1: Risk management does not remove the need for change control.
whyNot.2: Budget control stays within the project's governance, not with a supplier.
whyNot.3: Progress reporting is still needed; risk status is usually part of it.

C.q: Which TWO of the following are benefits of issue management? 1. Problems are escalated to someone with authority to act. 2. Issues are prevented from ever arising. 3. Impact is contained by prompt, owned action. 4. The sponsor is freed from all decisions.
options: 1 and 2
3 and 4
2 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Issue management gets problems to the right decision-maker (1) and limits their impact through prompt action (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issues will still arise. Preventing them is the job of risk management, and even that cannot stop them all.
whyNot.1: Statement 4 is wrong: issues beyond tolerance need the sponsor's decision.
whyNot.2: Both 2 and 4 are false claims about issue management.

C.q: Before releasing the next tranche of funding for a new ferry terminal, an investor asks to see the risk register and how the main risks are being handled. Which benefit of risk management is the investor mainly looking for?
options: Proof that the project has no threats
A guarantee that costs will not rise
Confidence that risks are under control
Evidence that issues cannot now happen
C.why: A well-run register shows that risks are understood, owned and being managed, which builds stakeholder confidence.

whyNot.0: Every project has threats; the register shows they are known, not absent.
whyNot.1: Risk management can't guarantee costs; it shows exposure is controlled.
whyNot.3: Issues can still occur; the register shows readiness, not immunity.

reteach.title: Think of planning an outdoor wedding
reteach.question: A couple is planning a summer wedding in a garden. What are the risks and issues, and what does managing them actually buy the couple?

blocks.h: Rain is a risk; a flat tyre on the day is an issue
blocks.body: Weeks before, rain is a RISK: it might happen. The couple books a marquee option and checks the forecast, so the day goes ahead whatever the weather. A cheaper caterer offering a discount if they book early is an OPPORTUNITY. On the morning, the bridal car's flat tyre is an ISSUE: it has happened, so someone with authority (the best man with a credit card) books a taxi immediately.

blocks.h: What managing them buys the couple

blocks.text: Even with perfect planning, something unexpected will happen. Risk management raises the chance of a good day; it doesn't guarantee one. That is why issue management is needed too.

explain.body: Risk: an uncertain event that would affect objectives if it occurred; a threat or an opportunity. Issue: something that has happened and needs action; beyond the PM's tolerance it goes to the sponsor.

rows.label: The supplier MAY go bust before delivery
A grant MAY cover part of the fit-out
The supplier HAS gone bust; kit not delivered

explain.note: Ask: has it happened yet? If not, it's a risk.

test.q: A council's new refuse lorries 'might arrive late if a strike at the factory goes ahead next month'. How should this be classified?
options: An issue
A threat risk
An opportunity
A constraint
test.why: The late delivery is uncertain and in the future, and it would harm objectives: a threat risk.

whyNot.0: Nothing has happened yet, so it is not an issue.
whyNot.2: The effect would be negative, so it is a threat, not an opportunity.
whyNot.3: A constraint is a fixed limit on the project, not an uncertain event.

explain.body: More likely to achieve objectives; fewer surprises; better decisions and plans; realistic contingency; a protected business case; opportunities exploited; stakeholder confidence.

explain.h: Hook: risk work makes plans SAFER

test.q: A logistics firm must choose between two warehouse sites. Analysing the risks of each before deciding mainly helps the firm to…
options: avoid writing a business case at all
compare the options on real exposure
remove every threat from both options
delay the decision until risks vanish
test.why: Better decisions are a key benefit: options can be compared on their risk exposure, not just their headline cost.

whyNot.0: Risk analysis informs the business case; it doesn't replace it.
whyNot.2: Threats can be reduced but not removed entirely.
whyNot.3: Risks rarely vanish; waiting for that would stall the project.

explain.body: Issues logged are visible and owned. Prompt analysis contains impact. Escalation beyond tolerance puts decisions at the right level. Resolutions go through change control. Patterns in the log reveal root causes.

explain.h: Why logging beats a quick informal fix

steps.label: Learned
steps.sub: Repeats point to a root cause

test.q: Why should a project's issues be formally logged rather than fixed informally as they arise?
options: So each is visible, owned and tracked
So the team can delay acting on them
So the PM can avoid telling the sponsor
So they can be reclassified as risks
test.why: Logging gives every issue visibility, an owner and a record through to closure, and lets patterns be spotted.

whyNot.1: Logging supports prompt action; delay lets impact grow.
whyNot.2: Issues beyond tolerance must reach the sponsor; logging makes that easier.
whyNot.3: An issue has already happened, so it can't become a risk again.

explain.body: Risks include upside. Recording opportunities means the team can plan to capture extra value if they arise. Managing threats and opportunities together protects, and can improve, the costs and benefits that justify the project.

test.q: A contractor on a school extension might finish the groundworks early, freeing the site two weeks sooner. Treated as an opportunity, what can risk management do with it?
options: Ignore it, as only threats matter
Log it as an issue for the sponsor to decide
Close it because it cannot cause harm
Plan to capture the benefit if it occurs
test.why: Opportunities are managed too: the team can plan, for example, to bring follow-on work forward if the site is freed early.

whyNot.0: Risk management covers threats and opportunities.
whyNot.1: It hasn't happened, so it isn't an issue.
whyNot.2: Opportunities stay open so their benefit can be captured; harmlessness isn't a reason to close them.
